items.title: Hölder spaces $C^{k,\alpha}$, closure and interior scaled norms, and $C^{k,\alpha}$ domains
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a function $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $C^k$ and the canonical-order derivatives $D^\beta u$ are those of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Put
$$[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}:=\sum_{|\beta|=k}\ \sup_{\substack{x,y\in\Omega\\ x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta u(x)-D^\beta u(y)|}{|x-y|^{\alpha}},\qquad \|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}\ \max_{|\beta|=j}|D^\beta u(x)|+[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega},$$
where the sums and maxima run over the finitely many multi-indices of the stated order. The quantity $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}$ is the **$k$-th order $\alpha$-Hölder seminorm** of $u$ and the quantity $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ the **$C^{k,\alpha}$ norm** of $u$; both are taken in $[0,+\infty]$, so the "norm" may be $+\infty$ and only the class below carries a genuine normed-space structure.

The **local Hölder class** $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega'}<+\infty$ for every $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$. The **bounded (closure) class** $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}<+\infty$. Thus $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)\subseteq C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and the inclusion may be strict: on $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the function $u(x)=\sin(|x|^2)$ lies in the local class (it is $C^1$, hence locally $\alpha$-Hölder on every compact set), while $[u]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^n}=+\infty$, because at the points $x_j=\sqrt{2\pi j}\,e_1$ and $y_j=x_j+(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{-1}e_1$ the difference quotients are $\asymp(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{\alpha}\to\infty$. On the bounded class the displayed formula is a norm, and the assignment $u\mapsto\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ is that norm.

**Scaled interior norm.** For a ball $B_R(x_0)\subseteq\Omega$ of radius $R>0$ and centre $x_0$, write $[v]_{0,\alpha;B}:=\sup\{|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^{\alpha}:x,y\in B,\ x\ne y\}$ for the plain Hölder seminorm on a set $B$, and put
$$\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}R^{j}\max_{|\beta|=j}\ \sup_{B_R(x_0)}|D^\beta u|+R^{k+\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=k}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}.$$
This is the **scaled interior norm** of $u$ on the ball; for $k=2$ it is exactly the scaled quantity of [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]], and it takes values in $[0,+\infty]$ as well. It is read off the open ball alone.

**Bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domains.** A **bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain** in $\mathbb R^n$ is a bounded nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with the following local graph property: for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal $Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and a function $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{y=(y',y_n)\in B\times\mathbb R:\ y_n<\varphi(y')\}.$$
This generalises the integer-order notion of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] to the Hölder scale, with the same one-sided graph convention; the regularity $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B)$ is the only strengthening, connectedness is not required, and no boundary seminorm is attached to the interior norms above. In dimension $n=1$ the corresponding sets are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals.

**The boundary-extension class.** Let $\Omega$ be bounded and let $u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Say that $u$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when each derivative field $D^\beta u$ with $|\beta|\le k$ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega$. The extension of each field is then unique, since $\Omega$ is dense in $\overline\Omega$, and the sup and Hölder quantities formed with the extended fields and suprema over $\overline\Omega$ agree with those displayed above, formed over $\Omega$: a supremum over the dense subset $\Omega$ already computes the supremum of the extension, and for the seminorm the inequality $[\tilde v]_{0,\alpha;\overline\Omega}\le[v]_{0,\alpha;\Omega}$ follows by approximating a pair in $\overline\Omega$ by pairs in $\Omega$, so the two seminorms are equal. We equip $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with this common norm. This is the Hölder-scale analogue of the interior-up-to-boundary convention for integer order $C^m(\overline\Omega)$ fixed in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]].
items.strategy: Collect the published ball-local notation of [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]] into the global local and closure scales, keeping the two apart: the local class may have $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}=\infty$ while the closure class is a normed space. Repeat the scaling computation of the published definition to fix the powers $R^j$ and $R^{k+\alpha}$ in the interior norm, and add the graph definition of a $C^{k,\alpha}$ boundary by analogy with [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Record that the definition asserts no regularity beyond the stated one, no boundary trace, and no choice principle beyond the ambient conventions.

items.title: The closure Hölder spaces are Banach spaces
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, $0<\alpha<1$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty. Then $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with the norm of [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]] is a Banach space over $\mathbb K$: every Cauchy sequence in $\|\cdot\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ converges in that norm to a limit whose $k$-th partial derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder on $\Omega$. If in addition $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain with nonempty boundary, then the subspace
$$X_0:=\{u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega): u\text{ extends continuously to }\bar\Omega\text{ with }u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$$
is closed in $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega)$ and hence is a Banach space. For every bounded open nonempty $\Omega$, the boundary-extension class $C^{k,\alpha}(\bar\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is also a closed subspace of $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and hence a Banach space, as is its zero-boundary subspace. Completeness here is for the full finite Hölder norm. A boundary Hölder seminorm alone does not define a norm on this function space, since it vanishes on nonzero constant functions.
items.strategy: Uniform Cauchy convergence gives bounded continuous limits of each derivative field. The one-variable derivative-limit theorem on coordinate segments, with mixed-partial symmetry, identifies these fields with the derivatives of the limiting function. Passing top-order difference quotients to the limit gives finite Holder seminorms and convergence of Cauchy differences in the full finite-component norm, proving completeness of C_b. On bounded open sets the boundary-extension class is a closed subspace: by density, the continuous extensions of every derivative field are uniformly Cauchy on the closure, and their continuous limits extend the limiting derivatives. Uniform convergence of the function extension preserves zero boundary values, so the zero-boundary subspaces are closed and Banach. The closure class need not equal C_b on arbitrary open sets. Countable Choice suffices.

items.title: The cancelled representation of the second derivatives of Newtonian potentials
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Phi$ be the fundamental solution normalised by $-\Delta\Phi=\delta_0$ on $\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]]); for $z\ne0$ put $k_{ij}(z):=\partial_i\partial_j\Phi(z)$ and write $V_{ij}f:=\mathrm{p.v.}(k_{ij}*f)$ as in [[def-calderon-zygmund-kernel-and-principal-value-operator]]. Then:

(i) $k_{ij}$ is smooth off $0$, homogeneous of degree $-n$, satisfies $|k_{ij}(z)|\le C_n|z|^{-n}$ and $|\nabla k_{ij}(z)|\le C_n|z|^{-n-1}$, and hence $|k_{ij}(z-h)-k_{ij}(z)|\le C_n|h||z|^{-n-1}$ whenever $|z|\ge2|h|$; its mean over every centred sphere is zero, so it is a standard Hölder Calderón–Zygmund kernel in the sense of [[def-standard-holder-calderon-zygmund-kernel]].

(ii) For every $f\in C^{0,\alpha}_c(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0<\alpha\le1$, $Nf$ has classical second derivatives and, for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\partial_i\partial_jNf(x)=\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int_{\mathbb R^n} k_{ij}(x-y)f(y)\,dy-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{n}f(x)=\int_{|x-y|<1}k_{ij}(x-y)(f(y)-f(x))\,dy+\int_{|x-y|\ge1}k_{ij}(x-y)f(y)\,dy-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{n}f(x).$$
Both displayed ordinary integrals converge absolutely: the first by Hölder continuity at the singularity, the second because it avoids the singularity and $f$ is compactly supported. The local subtraction is only over the unit ball; the globally subtracted integrand $k_{ij}(x-y)(f(y)-f(x))$ is not absolutely integrable over $\mathbb R^n$ when $f(x)\ne0$, since $k_{ij}(r\theta)=r^{-n}k_{ij}(\theta)$, its nonzero continuous angular factor has positive spherical $L^1$ norm, and $\int_1^\infty r^{-1}dr=\infty$, so no global Lebesgue integral replaces the principal value.

(iii) As a tempered distribution, $D_{ij}\Phi=\mathrm{p.v.}\,k_{ij}-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{n}\delta_0$; consequently, for every $f\in L^\infty_c(\mathbb R^n)$, the distributional second derivative of $Nf$ is given by the truncated pairings,
$$\partial_i\partial_jNf=\mathrm{p.v.}(k_{ij}*f)-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{n}f\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n),$$
that is, $\langle\partial_i\partial_jNf,\varphi\rangle=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\iint_{|x-y|\ge\varepsilon}k_{ij}(x-y)f(y)\varphi(x)\,dy\,dx-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{n}\int f\varphi$ for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$.
items.strategy: Differentiate the distributional identity for the fundamental solution: the boundary term from excising $B_\varepsilon(0)$ converges to $-(\delta_{ij}/n)\delta_0$, since $\int_{S^{n-1}}\omega_i\omega_j\,d\sigma=(|S^{n-1}|/n)\delta_{ij}$. This gives $D_{ij}\Phi=\mathrm{p.v.}\,k_{ij}-(\delta_{ij}/n)\delta_0$. Computing the radial derivatives gives homogeneity, the size and gradient bounds, and the zero spherical mean. Convolving the distributional identity with $f$ gives the principal-value formula. On $|x-y|<1$, subtract $f(x)$ and use the zero spherical mean; leave the far-field integral unsubtracted. Near $x$, its absolute integrand is $O(|x-y|^{\alpha-n})$; away from $x$ it is integrable because $f$ is compactly supported. This is the local cancellation form of Hunter Theorem 2.26/Corollary 2.27, not a global subtraction identity.

items.title: Uniformly elliptic nondivergence-form operators and their frozen coefficients
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A **second-order nondivergence-form operator** on $\Omega$ is an expression
$$Lu=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_ju+b^i\partial_iu+cu,$$
with real-valued bounded measurable coefficients $a^{ij},b^i,c$ on $\Omega$ and summation over the repeated indices $i,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. In this operator notation, coordinates and coordinate partials are relabelled from [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]: coordinate $i$ and $\partial_i$ here mean coordinate $i-1$ and $\partial_{i-1}$ there, and likewise $\xi_i$ means component $i-1$ of $\xi$. Multi-index derivatives $D^\beta$ retain that dependency's zero-based canonical order. The expression acts on functions for which the displayed classical derivatives exist. The matrix field $A=(a^{ij})_{i,j=1}^{n}$ is the **principal coefficient matrix**, and $(b^i)$ and $c$ are the **lower-order coefficients**.

The operator is **uniformly elliptic** on $\Omega$ with constants $0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty$ when $A(x)$ is symmetric for almost every $x\in\Omega$ and
$$\lambda|\xi|^2\le a^{ij}(x)\xi_i\xi_j\le\Lambda|\xi|^2$$
for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$ and almost every $x\in\Omega$. The number $\Lambda/\lambda\ge1$ is the **ellipticity ratio**; uniform ellipticity is a condition on the pointwise spectrum of $A$.

For $x_0\in\Omega$ the **frozen operator** at $x_0$ is the constant-coefficient operator $L_{x_0}:=a^{ij}(x_0)\partial_i\partial_j$ built from the principal matrix at the single point $x_0$; when the coefficients are continuous at $x_0$ the frozen operator is to be regarded as the constant-coefficient model of $L$ near $x_0$. When the principal coefficients are of class $C^{0,\alpha}$ with respect to [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]] on a ball $B\subseteq\Omega$, one writes $[A]_{0,\alpha;B}\le K$ for the maximum over $i,j$ of the Hölder seminorms $[a^{ij}]_{0,\alpha;B}$, and when $\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty\le M$ on $B$ one says that the lower-order coefficients of $L$ are bounded by $M$ on $B$.
items.strategy: Introduce the operator and the ellipticity condition in the nondivergence form actually used by the Schauder and $W^{2,p}$ estimates, together with the frozen-coefficient notation. Keep the coefficient classes explicit, since the two halves of this page use different regimes ($C^{0,\alpha}$ for Schauder, continuous for $W^{2,p}$) and the drift note forbids silently claiming a VMO regime. No choice principle is needed for the definition.

items.title: Ehrling-type Hölder and derivative interpolation with an epsilon loss
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, $0<\alpha<1$, let $k\ge1$ be an integer, $R>0$, and let $B_R\subseteq\Omega$ be a ball in an open set. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C=C(n,k,\alpha,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that every $u$ with $\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R}<\infty$ satisfies
$$\text{(i)}\quad\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}R^j\max_{|\beta|=j}\ \sup_{B_R}|D^\beta u|\le\varepsilon\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R}+C\sup_{B_R}|u|,$$
$$\text{(ii)}\quad\max_{|\beta|=k}\ \sup_{B_R}|D^\beta u|\le\varepsilon R^{\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=k}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha;B_R}+CR^{-k}\sup_{B_R}|u|.$$
For $0<\alpha<\beta\le1$ and $f\in C^{0,\beta}(B_R)$, one also has
$$\text{(iii)}\quad[f]_{0,\alpha;B_R}\le\varepsilon R^{\beta-\alpha}[f]_{0,\beta;B_R}+C(n,\alpha,\beta)\varepsilon^{-\alpha/(\beta-\alpha)}R^{-\alpha}\sup_{B_R}|f|.$$
The constants are independent of $u,f,R$; the inequalities are scale-invariant.
items.strategy: Rescale to $B_1$ using the scaling identity in [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]]. For (iii), split pairs at distance $h$, bound the short increments by $2\|f\|_\infty h^{-\alpha}$ and the long increments by $[f]_{0,\beta}h^{\beta-\alpha}$, and choose $h$ so the latter coefficient is $\varepsilon R^{\beta-\alpha}$; the resulting constant depends on $\beta$ and has the stated power of $\varepsilon$. For (i)-(ii), use Taylor's formula along segments to control lower derivatives by $\|u\|_\infty$ and $\|D^ku\|_\infty$, then apply (iii) with $\beta=1$ to the top derivative and absorb. This is the scale-normalized Ehrling argument of [S] Exercises 8.4-8.6.

items.title: Freezing coefficients makes the Schauder error absorbable on a small ball
items.statement:
Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$ and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$. Let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty$, $[A]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\le K$, and $b,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$. Put $L_0:=a^{ij}(x_0)\partial_i\partial_j$ and
$$\mathfrak M_R:=R^\alpha K+R\|b\|_\infty+R^{1+\alpha}[b]_{0,\alpha}+R^2\|c\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[c]_{0,\alpha}.$$
Assume $\mathfrak M_R<\infty$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $\eta_\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ and $C_\varepsilon<\infty$, depending only on $n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda,\mathfrak M_R,\varepsilon$, such that for every radius $0<\rho\le R\eta_\varepsilon$ and every $u$ with $\|u\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_\rho(x_0)}<\infty$,
$$\rho^2\|(L-L_0)u\|^{*}_{0,\alpha;B_\rho(x_0)}\le\varepsilon\|u\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_\rho(x_0)}+C_\varepsilon\sup_{B_\rho(x_0)}|u|,$$
where the cutoff $R\eta_\varepsilon$ is at most $R$ and the constant is uniform over all smaller radii, and $\|g\|^{*}_{0,\alpha;B_\rho}:=\sup_{B_\rho}|g|+\rho^\alpha[g]_{0,\alpha;B_\rho}$.
items.strategy: Normalize to the unit ball, estimate the Hölder products for the frozen principal error and lower-order terms on every radius t below a chosen threshold, and use interpolation to make the full scaled C^{2,α} coefficient as small as prescribed while keeping the sup-norm remainder uniformly bounded.

items.title: Interior Schauder estimate for uniformly elliptic equations
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, $[A]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\le K$, and $b,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ with finite global Hölder seminorms. Let $u\in C^2(B_R(x_0))\cap L^\infty(B_R(x_0))$ satisfy $Lu=f$ pointwise with $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$. Then $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(B_{R/2}(x_0))$ and
$$\|u\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_{R/2}(x_0)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\bigr),$$
where $C$ depends only on $n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the finite dimensionless coefficient bounds $R^\alpha K+R\|b\|_\infty+R^{1+\alpha}[b]_{0,\alpha}+R^2\|c\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[c]_{0,\alpha}$.
items.strategy: Prove finite local C2,alpha regularity by frozen mean-zero potential replacement, harmonic excess decay and telescoping Campanato means. Apply the conditional local estimate only afterward. Retain the separated-pair Hessian-sup term; interpolate at a parameter proportional to the shrinking radius to the power alpha. This yields a uniform seminorm contraction with data growth radius^(-(2+alpha)); iterate and recover lower derivatives by fixed-parameter interpolation.

items.title: $C^{2,\alpha}$ boundary flattening preserves the nondivergence structure, ellipticity and Hölder norms
items.statement:
Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$ and let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain. For every $x_0\in\partial\Omega$, after a rigid motion and possibly reversing the last coordinate, there are $r>0$ and $\varphi\in C^{2,\alpha}(Q'_r)$, $Q'_r=(-r,r)^{n-1}$, with $\varphi(0)=0$, $D\varphi(0)=0$, such that for $Q_r=Q'_r\times(-r,r)$ the shear $\Psi(y',y_n)=(y',y_n+\varphi(y'))$ is a diffeomorphism onto the patch $U:=\Psi(Q_r)$ and
$$\Psi(Q_r^+)=U\cap\Omega,\qquad \Psi(Q'_r\times\{0\})=U\cap\partial\Omega,$$
where $Q_r^+=Q'_r\times(0,r)$. In particular the chart is stated on its actual image patch; no equality with the intersection of a Euclidean ball and $\Omega$ is asserted. Composition with $\Psi$ gives equivalent $C^{2,\alpha}$ norms on the closures of $U\cap\Omega$ and $Q_r^+$, with constants depending on the chart. If $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ has $C^{0,\alpha}$ coefficients on $U$, then its pullback under $v=u\circ\Psi$ is again nondivergence form with $C^{0,\alpha}$ coefficients. Its principal matrix is
$$\widetilde A(y)=D\Psi(y)^{-1}A(\Psi(y))D\Psi(y)^{-T},$$
so its ellipticity constants may be taken as $\lambda\|D\Psi\|_\infty^{-2}$ and $\Lambda\|D\Psi^{-1}\|_\infty^2$; the lower-order coefficients are given by the chain rule and have Hölder bounds controlled by the chart and original coefficient norms.
items.strategy:
Use the graph chart from [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] and define the physical patch to be $U=\Psi(Q_r)$; this makes the half-cylinder and boundary-face identities exact despite the curved graph. For $v=u\circ\Psi$, the chain rule gives $Du(\Psi)=D\Psi^{-T}Dv$ and
$$D^2u(\Psi)=D\Psi^{-T}\bigl(D^2v-Du(\Psi)\cdot D^2\Psi\bigr)D\Psi^{-1}.$$
Consequently the principal matrix is $D\Psi^{-1}(A\circ\Psi)D\Psi^{-T}$, not $D\Psi(A\circ\Psi)D\Psi^T$. The singular-value bounds give $\lambda/\|D\Psi\|_\infty^2$ below and $\Lambda\|D\Psi^{-1}\|_\infty^2$ above. The remaining chain-rule terms involve $D^2\Psi$ and $D\Psi^{-1}$, whose stated Hölder bounds preserve the lower-order coefficient regularity. Apply the same composition estimates to $\Psi^{-1}$ for the reverse norm inequality; this is the flattening step of [V] §3.1.1 and [Si] Lecture 12.

items.title: Boundary Schauder estimate for the Dirichlet problem
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $\bar\Omega$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, $[A]_{0,\alpha;\Omega}\le K$, and $b,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ with $\|b\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|c\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\le M$. Let $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^0(\bar\Omega)$, $g\in C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ and $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ satisfy $Lu=f$ in $\Omega$ and $u=g$ on $\partial\Omega$. Then $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{C^0(\Omega)}+\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}+\|g\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}\bigr),$$
where $C=C(n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda,K,M,\Omega)$ depends on $\Omega$ only through a finite $C^{2,\alpha}$ chart atlas and its radii. The coefficient assumptions include the H\"older norms needed for the lower-order products, and no solvability is asserted: the estimate is a regularity statement for the given classical solution.
items.strategy: Subtract g, extend closure coefficients locally by chart reflection and flatten the boundary. Apply the quoted Gilbarg-Trudinger boundary regularity upgrade before the Simon a priori half-patch estimate. Cover the compact closure with ambient boundary patches and interior balls. A Lebesgue number handles near pairs and derivative suprema handle distant pairs; no intermediate-norm absorption is used here.

items.title: The method of continuity for a uniformly estimated affine family of bounded operators
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces over the same field, let $L_0,L_1\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ and put $L_t:=(1-t)L_0+tL_1$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Assume (i) $L_0$ is bijective; (ii) there is $C<\infty$ with the uniform a priori estimate $\|x\|_X\le C\|L_tx\|_Y$ for every $t\in[0,1]$ and every $x\in X$. Then $L_t$ is bijective for every $t\in[0,1]$, and $\|L_t^{-1}\|_{Y\to X}\le C$ for every $t$. No compactness or reflexivity hypothesis is used: the uniform estimate alone makes the bijectivity set closed, and the Neumann series makes it open.
items.strategy: Let $I:=\{t\in[0,1]:L_t\text{ bijective}\}$. Injectivity always follows from (ii), and $0\in I$ by (i). Closedness: if $t_j\to t$ with $t_j\in I$ and $f\in Y$, put $u_j:=L_{t_j}^{-1}f$; then $\|u_j-u_k\|_X\le C\|L_{t_j}(u_j-u_k)\|_Y=C\|(L_{t_k}-L_{t_j})u_k\|_Y\le C|t_k-t_j|\,\|L_1-L_0\|\,\|u_k\|_X\le C^2|t_k-t_j|\,\|L_1-L_0\|\,\|f\|_Y$, so $(u_j)$ is Cauchy and converges to some $u\in X$; then $L_tu=\lim_j\bigl(L_{t_j}u_j+(L_t-L_{t_j})u_j\bigr)=f$. Openness: if $t\in I$ then (ii) gives $\|L_t^{-1}y\|_X\le C\|y\|_Y$, and for $|s-t|<1/(C\|L_1-L_0\|)$ the identity $L_s=L_t\bigl(I+L_t^{-1}(L_s-L_t)\bigr)$ with $\|L_t^{-1}(L_s-L_t)\bigr\|<1$ makes $L_s$ bijective by [[lem-neumann-series-and-small-perturbations-of-bounded-inverses]]. Hence $I$ is nonempty, open and closed in $[0,1]$, so $I=[0,1]$.

items.title: Global $W^{2,p}$ estimate for the Laplacian on Euclidean space
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and $1<p<\infty$. Then there is $C=C(n,p)<\infty$ such that every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfies
$$\|D^2u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|\Delta u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)},\qquad \|\partial_i\partial_ju\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|\Delta u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)},$$
for all $i,j$, where $\|D^2u\|_{L^p}:=\max_{|\beta|=2}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p}$; by density the bound extends to every $u\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ (for which $\Delta u\in L^p$ holds automatically). The constant may be taken as the square of the Riesz-transform bound of [[cor-riesz-transforms-are-bounded-on-lp]], hence is finite throughout $1<p<\infty$, including $p=2$. No sharp endpoint growth rate is claimed.
items.strategy: For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$, the Fourier multiplier identity is $\partial_i\partial_j u=R_iR_j(-\Delta u)$ with the library's Riesz-transform convention. The strict-range $L^p$ bounds for $R_i$ and $R_j$ in [[cor-riesz-transforms-are-bounded-on-lp]] therefore give both displayed estimates directly. This is the proof route in [S] §7.6 and [V] Theorem 3.7; it uses an $L^2$-anchored Riesz transform theorem and does not infer an $L^p$ bound from kernel size alone. Density extends the estimate to $W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^n)$.

items.title: $L^p$ interpolation absorption of first derivatives by second derivatives
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$ and $1<p<\infty$, and for a function with the relevant weak derivatives write $\|Du\|_{L^p}:=\max_{|\beta|=1}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p}$ and $\|D^2u\|_{L^p}:=\max_{|\beta|=2}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p}$, equivalent to the sum-form Sobolev norms of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] up to constants depending on $n$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C=C(n,p,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that every $u\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfies
$$\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le\varepsilon\|D^2u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}+C\|u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}.$$
The scaled form on balls, with the norm over the doubled ball on the right, is
$$\|Du\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}\le\varepsilon R\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_{2R}(x_0))}+C R^{-1}\|u\|_{L^p(B_{2R}(x_0))}\qquad\bigl(u\in W^{2,p}(B_{2R}(x_0))\bigr),$$
with $C$ independent of $R$ and $x_0$. This is the absorption inequality used in the frozen-coefficient $W^{2,p}$ estimates. The result is asserted for the strict range $1<p<\infty$ only; the form with the same ball on both sides is not claimed here.
items.strategy: For $u\in C_c^\infty$ write the symbol of $\partial_i$ as $i\xi_i=\frac{i\xi_i}{\varepsilon|\xi|^2+1}\cdot(\varepsilon|\xi|^2+1)$; the multiplier $m_\varepsilon(\xi):=\xi_i/(\varepsilon|\xi|^2+1)$ is smooth off the origin and satisfies the Mihlin bounds $|\xi|^{|\beta|}|\partial^\beta m_\varepsilon(\xi)|\le C_\beta\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ for every multi-index $\beta$, as the scaling identity $m_\varepsilon(\xi)=\varepsilon^{-1/2}m_1(\varepsilon^{1/2}\xi)$ shows, so [[thm-mihlin-fourier-multiplier-theorem]] gives $\|T_{m_\varepsilon}g\|_p\le C_{n,p}\varepsilon^{-1/2}\|g\|_p$. Applying this with $g=\varepsilon(-\Delta u)+u$ gives $\|\partial_iu\|_p\le C_{n,p}\bigl(\sqrt\varepsilon\|\Delta u\|_p+\varepsilon^{-1/2}\|u\|_p\bigr)$, and renaming $\sqrt\varepsilon$ yields the claim; the ball form follows by rescaling $u_R(z)=u(x_0+Rz)$. The general $W^{2,p}$ case follows by density [[thm-meyers-serrin-density-on-an-arbitrary-open-set]], and the classical Gagliardo–John–Nirenberg inequality is the equivalent elementary route of [V] (3.16).

items.title: The cutoff commutator in the local $W^{2,p}$ estimates
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $1<p<\infty$, $R>0$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ have bounded coefficients on $B_R(x_0)$ with $|A|\le\Lambda$, $|b|\le M_b$ and $|c|\le M_c$, where $|A|:=\max_{i,j}|a^{ij}|$. Let $\eta\in C_c^\infty(B_R(x_0))$ satisfy $|D\eta|\le C_1R^{-1}$ and $|D^2\eta|\le C_2R^{-2}$, and let $u\in W^{2,p}(B_R(x_0))$. Then almost everywhere
$$L(\eta u)=\eta\,Lu+(a^{ij}+a^{ji})(\partial_i\eta)\partial_ju+\bigl(a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j\eta+b^i\partial_i\eta\bigr)u,$$
and consequently
$$\|L(\eta u)-\eta\,Lu\|_{L^p}\le C_n\Bigl(\Lambda C_1R^{-1}\|Du\|_{L^p}+\bigl(\Lambda C_2R^{-2}+M_bC_1R^{-1}\bigr)\|u\|_{L^p}\Bigr).$$
There is no second derivative of $u$ in the commutator.
No symmetry assumption on the principal coefficient matrix $A=(a^{ij})$ is needed.
items.strategy: Apply the weak-derivative product rule twice. For a general coefficient matrix, the two principal cross terms combine to $(a^{ij}+a^{ji})(\partial_i\eta)\partial_j u$; entrywise bounds give at most $2\Lambda n^2 C_1R^{-1}|Du|$, absorbed by $C_n$. The second-order cutoff and drift terms have bounds $\Lambda n^2C_2R^{-2}|u|$ and $M_bnC_1R^{-1}|u|$, while the zeroth-order term cancels. No symmetry of $A$ is used.

items.title: Local $W^{2,p}$ regularity of weak solutions of the Poisson equation
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<\infty$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a ball and let $u\in W^{1,2}(B)$ satisfy $-\Delta u=f$ in the distributional sense on $B$ with $f\in L^p(B)$. Then $u\in W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, and for every open $B'\Subset B$ there is $C=C(n,p,B',B)<\infty$ with
$$\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(B')}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{L^p(B)}+\|u\|_{L^2(B)}\bigr).$$
No boundary regularity is asserted, and no decay of $u$ at infinity is assumed; the estimate is local in the interior only.
items.strategy: Localize the forcing, estimate smooth Newtonian Hessians using growing cutoffs and the whole-space Laplacian estimate, and pass the cutoff radius to infinity. Approximate general Lp data with one common compact support; completeness and distributional continuity identify the Hessian limit. Retain support-radius dependence in the local Young bounds. Subtract the potential and control the harmonic remainder by its L1 norm and the given L2 norm.

items.title: Interior $W^{2,p}$ estimate for uniformly elliptic equations with continuous coefficients
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<\infty$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, continuous principal coefficients on the closed ball, and $\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty\le M$. Then every $u\in W^{2,p}(B_R(x_0))$ with $Lu=f\in L^p$ satisfies the scale-invariant estimate
$$\sum_{j=0}^{2}R^{j-2}\max_{|\beta|=j}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p(B_{R/2}(x_0))}\le C\bigl(R^{-2}\|u\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}+\|f\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}\bigr),$$
where $D^0u=u$ and the maximum runs over multi-indices of order $j$,
where $C$ may depend on $n,p,\lambda,\Lambda,R\|b\|_\infty,R^2\|c\|_\infty$ and the modulus of continuity of $A$ on the ball. A radius-independent constant requires uniform control of these dimensionless lower-order bounds and of the modulus. The theorem assumes continuity of $A$; no estimate for merely measurable principal coefficients is asserted.
items.strategy: Freeze the principal matrix on small balls, localize with cutoffs equal to one on smaller balls, use the whole-space constant-coefficient estimate and the doubled-ball interpolation inequality, and absorb coefficient oscillation. A finite-overlap lattice cover gives the local Hessian estimate. Run the hole-filling recurrence from radius $3R/4$ up to $R$, so the Hessian is controlled on $B_{3R/4}$. Then cover $B_{R/2}$ by fixed-radius inner balls whose doubled balls lie in $B_{3R/4}$; the doubled-ball interpolation inequality on this cover controls the weighted first-derivative term. Combining the Hessian, gradient and zeroth-order estimates yields the scale-invariant weighted $W^{2,p}$ estimate.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Then there is $C<\infty$, depending on $n,p,\lambda,\Lambda,M,\Omega$ and the modulus of continuity of $A$, such that every $u\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ satisfies
$$\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|Lu\|_{L^p(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\bigr).$$
The estimate is a priori and asserts neither solvability nor weak-to-strong regularity: the function is assumed to lie in $W^{2,p}$ with zero trace.

Near the boundary, flatten C^{1,1} graph charts; the transformed principal matrix has modulus bounded by C(ω_A(Cr)+r), including the chart Jacobian variation. Apply the constant-coefficient half-space Dirichlet estimate to a cutoff, use odd extension and doubled-ball interpolation for the cutoff terms, and choose each local Hessian error after the finite-overlap constant is fixed. An ℓ^p sum over the bounded-overlap cover makes the final error absorbable. The C^{1,1} composition/weak chain rule is proved locally by the a.e. chain rule, bounded second chart derivatives, change of variables, and smooth approximation.

items.title: Global Schauder regularity for the weak Dirichlet Laplacian
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice together with Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$,
$0<\alpha<1$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain, let
$f\in C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ and $g\in C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$. Then
the weak Dirichlet problem $-\Delta u=f$ in $\Omega$, $u=g$ on
$\partial\Omega$ (understood as $u-g\in H^1_0(\Omega)$) has exactly one
solution $u\in H^1(\Omega)$, and this solution belongs to
$C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$, satisfies $-\Delta u=f$ pointwise in $\Omega$
and $u=g$ on $\partial\Omega$, and obeys
$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}+\|g\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}\bigr)$$
with $C=C(n,\alpha,\Omega)$. This supplies the Laplace base point of the
continuity method rather than assuming it.
items.strategy: Reduce to zero trace, extend and mollify the Hölder datum, and solve smooth approximating problems. The weak-to-strong supplier’s finite-exponent bootstrap gives uniform W^{2,p} bounds including the L^p term; embedding gives C^{1,gamma} representatives up to the boundary. Subtract a local Newtonian potential for interior smoothness, compare each real component using Delta(v-q)=M-F_epsilon>=0 and Delta(-v-q)=M+F_epsilon>=0, apply the boundary Schauder estimate, and pass to a C^2 limit by vector-valued Arzela-Ascoli. Uniqueness identifies the limit with the weak solution.

items.title: Global Schauder estimate and classical Dirichlet solvability by the continuity method
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $\bar\Omega$, with $a^{ij},b^i,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$, constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, $[A]_{0,\alpha}\le K$, and $\|b\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|c\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\le M$. Put $X:=\{u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega):u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$ and $L_t:=tL+(1-t)\Delta$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Assume that each $L_t:X\to C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ is injective. Then every $L_t$ is bijective; in particular every $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ and $g\in C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ determine a unique classical solution of $Lu=f$ in $\Omega$, $u=g$ on $\partial\Omega$, and
$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}+\|g\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}\bigr),$$
where $C$ is uniform in $t,u,f,g$.
items.strategy: The zero-boundary space $X$ is Banach and $t\mapsto L_t$ is continuous in operator norm. The base map $L_0=\Delta$ is bijective because [[thm-global-schauder-regularity-for-the-weak-dirichlet-laplacian]] solves $-\Delta$; multiplication by $-1$ transfers that result to $\Delta$. Boundary Schauder estimates give a uniform bound in terms of $\|L_tu\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u\|_{C^0}$. If no uniform estimate $\|u\|_X\le C\|L_tu\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$ held, choose $t_j\to t$ and $u_j$ with $\|u_j\|_X=1$ and $\|L_{t_j}u_j\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\to0$. Arzelà--Ascoli gives a subsequence converging in $C^2(\bar\Omega)$ to $u$, and continuity of the coefficients gives $L_tu=0$ with zero boundary values. Injectivity forces $u=0$, hence $\|u_j\|_{C^0}\to0$. Applying the uniform boundary Schauder estimate to $u_j$ now gives $\|u_j\|_X\to0$, contradicting the normalization. The method-of-continuity theorem then makes every $L_t$ bijective; subtract a $C^{2,\alpha}$ extension of $g$ for nonzero boundary data. This contradiction uses the full Schauder estimate to control the Hölder seminorm and does not infer seminorm convergence from uniform convergence.

items.title: Injectivity removes the $L^p$ term from the global $W^{2,p}$ estimate
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<\infty$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^{1,1}$ domain and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic with $a^{ij}\in C^0(\bar\Omega)$, $b,c\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ as in [[thm-global-w-two-p-dirichlet-estimate]]. Assume that the homogeneous Dirichlet problem has only the trivial strong solution: if $w\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ and $Lw=0$ almost everywhere, then $w=0$. Then there is $C<\infty$ with
$$\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|Lu\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\qquad\text{for every }u\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega).$$
No symmetry of $L$ is used and no spectral hypothesis beyond the stated injectivity enters; the constant can additionally depend on the particular operator $L$ through its separation from a nontrivial Dirichlet kernel. Injectivity alone supplies no bound uniform over all operators with the same coefficient upper bounds. The Axiom of Choice is needed because the compactness alternatives of Rellich--Kondrachov are invoked.
items.strategy: Suppose the inequality fails; then there are $u_j\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ with $\|u_j\|_{W^{2,p}}=1$ and $\|Lu_j\|_{L^p}\to0$. A bounded $W^{2,p}$ sequence is bounded in $W^{1,p}$, so the Rellich–Kondrachov compactness theorems ([[thm-rellich-kondrachov-for-p-less-than-n]] for $p<n$, [[thm-rellich-kondrachov-at-the-critical-source-exponent]] for $p=n$, [[thm-morrey-rellich-compactness-for-p-greater-than-n]] for $p>n$) give a subsequence converging in $L^p$; the a priori estimate [[thm-global-w-two-p-dirichlet-estimate]] applied to the differences makes $(u_j)$ Cauchy in $W^{2,p}$. Its limit $w$ lies in $W^{2,p}\cap W^{1,p}_0$, has $Lw=0$, hence $w=0$ by injectivity, and then the a priori estimate gives $\|u_j\|_{W^{2,p}}\le C(\|Lu_j\|_p+\|u_j\|_p)\to0$, contradicting $\|u_j\|_{W^{2,p}}=1$. This is the standard compactness argument recorded in [S] §8.9 and [V] Part III.

items.title: $W^{2,p}$ regularity implies classical or H"older regularity when $p$ is large
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<\infty$, and let $\Omega$ be
a bounded $W^{2,p}$-extension domain (the extension property is for this
displayed $k=2$ and exponent $p$). (i) If $p>n/2$, every
$u\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)$ has a representative in $C^{0,\gamma}(\bar\Omega)$
for every $0<\gamma<\min\{1,2-n/p\}$, with the norm controlled by
$\|u\|_{W^{2,p}}$. (ii) If $p>n$, every such $u$ has a representative in
$C^{1,\gamma}(\bar\Omega)$ for every $0<\gamma<1-n/p$, with the
corresponding norm bound; in particular $D^2u\in L^p$. For any
nondivergence expression $Lu=\sum_{|\beta|\le2}a_\beta D^\beta u$ with
$a_\beta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$, this gives $Lu\in L^p(\Omega)$; whenever
$Lu=f$ also holds distributionally for some $f\in L^p(\Omega)$, the equality
then holds almost everywhere. (iii) If $p>n/(1-\alpha)$ for $0<\alpha<1$,
the representative is $C^{1,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$. No finite $p$ gives
$C^{2,\alpha}$ regularity in general: on a ball, the function
$u(x)=(x_1)_+^2$ belongs to $W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$, while
$D_{11}u=2\mathbf 1_{\{x_1>0\}}$ has no continuous representative.
items.strategy: Apply the bounded-domain higher-order Sobolev embedding directly on the stated bounded W^{2,p}-extension domain, with k=2 and q=p. The three regularity clauses are the m=0, m=1 and fractional exponent cases of its supercritical branch. For sharpness use u=(x_1)_+^2 on the unit ball, a bounded smooth extension domain: its weak second derivative jumps across an interior disk, so it has no continuous representative for any finite p.

items.title: The Schauder and $W^{2,p}$ scales are different, not interchangeable
items.statement:
On a bounded domain, $C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ embeds strictly into $W^{2,p}(\Omega)$ for every finite $p$, and there is no reverse inclusion. Thus the spaces are not equivalent at top order. The estimate theorems on this page also use different forcing-data hypotheses, as item (iii) records.

- (i) **Inclusion $C^{2,\alpha}\subseteq W^{2,p}$ for all finite $p$.** If $\Omega$ is bounded and $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$, then each derivative $D^\beta u$ with $|\beta|\le2$ is continuous on the compact set $\bar\Omega$, and
  $$\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}\le|\Omega|^{1/p}\sum_{|\beta|\le2}\sup_\Omega|D^\beta u|\le C(\Omega)\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)},$$
  so $C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)\subseteq W^{2,p}(\Omega)$ with a norm bound depending on the volume and on $p$ through $|\Omega|^{1/p}$; the inclusion is strict, and the Schauder scale is the stronger hypothesis at the top order.
- (ii) **No reverse inclusion for any finite $p$.** For every $1<p<\infty$ the space $W^{2,p}(\Omega)$ is not contained in $C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$: on the unit ball the function $u(x)=(x_1)_+^2$ belongs to $W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$ while $D_{11}u=2\mathbf 1_{\{x_1>0\}}$ is discontinuous, as recorded with proof in [[cor-w-two-p-regularity-implies-classical-or-holder-regularity-when-p-is-large]]. More generally, under the Axiom of Choice, for $n\ge2$, and on a bounded $W^{2,p}$-extension domain, the Sobolev embedding gives at most one H\"older derivative, with exponent strictly below $1-n/p$ when $p>n$; finite $p$ never gives the two-derivative H\"older estimate.
- (iii) **The data classes differ in the same direction.** The $W^{2,p}$ estimate of [[thm-interior-w-two-p-estimate-for-uniformly-elliptic-equations]] accepts forcing $Lu\in L^p$ and concludes an $L^p$ bound for $D^2u$, while the Schauder estimate of [[thm-interior-schauder-estimate-for-uniformly-elliptic-equations]] requires $Lu\in C^{0,\alpha}$ and concludes a H\"older bound; since $C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)\subseteq L^p(\Omega)$ on a bounded domain with equality false, the Schauder theorem assumes strictly more on the data and concludes strictly more on the solution.
- (iv) **The endpoints are genuine restrictions of the two theories.** The strict range $0<\alpha<1$ in the Schauder scale is not a technicality: at the endpoint $\alpha=1$ the interior estimate fails, and the sharp modulus of $D^2Nf$ for a Lipschitz source is $|x||\log|x||$ rather than $|x|$, with the explicit witness recorded on the companion page ([[cex-schauder-estimates-fail-at-the-holder-endpoint-alpha-one]]). The range $1<p<\infty$ is the range of the Riesz-multiplier and singular-integral arguments used on this page for the Sobolev estimates; no endpoint $p=1$ or $p=\infty$ version is asserted here.
- (v) **Neither scale is a boundary regularity theorem by itself.** The $W^{2,p}$ estimate is a priori and assumes $u\in W^{2,p}$; a weak solution on a merely Lipschitz domain can fail to reach $W^{2,p}$ altogether at a reentrant corner ([[cex-boundary-w-two-p-regularity-needs-c-one-one-type-control]]), and the radius bookkeeping of both estimates is exercised by [[ex-schauder-scaling-on-a-quadratic-poisson-solution]].

Thus the two scales should be used according to the data: rough $L^p$ forcing is treated by the Sobolev scale at the price of losing H\"older regularity at the top order, while $C^{0,\alpha}$ forcing with controlled coefficients is treated by the Schauder scale, which gives two H\"older derivatives but no improvement at the endpoint $\alpha=1$ and no statement for rough coefficients.
items.strategy: Record the asymmetric comparison: the bounded-domain inclusion is strict in one direction, with no reverse inclusion, and the estimate theorems use different data hypotheses. The inclusion $C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)\subset W^{2,p}(\Omega)$ on a bounded domain is immediate from the definition of the closure norm and finiteness of the volume; the failure of the reverse inclusion follows from the exact embedding exponents of [[cor-w-two-p-regularity-implies-classical-or-holder-regularity-when-p-is-large]]. The assertion is a remark and carries no proof obligation of its own; the companion examples page holds the corresponding counterexamples for both endpoints.

items.title: Weak global $W^{2,p}$ regularity for the Dirichlet Laplacian
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $n<p<\infty$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain for some $0<\alpha<1$. If $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $-\Delta u=f$ with $f\in L^p(\Omega)$, then $u\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{L^p(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\bigr),$$
where $C=C(n,p,\Omega)$. This is a weak-to-strong regularity theorem; the estimate applies to the weak solution only after its $W^{2,p}$ membership has been established, and the assumption $p>n$ is the range in which the bootstrap of Sobolev exponents terminates at $p$.
items.strategy: Choose a real $\lambda>0$ larger than the $\lambda_0$ in Haller-Dintelmann Theorem 19.7 for the finitely many exponents used below. The bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain is a $W^{k,q}$ extension domain for each finite $q$, so [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]] applies. Initially $u\in H^1_0$ gives $u\in L^{q_0}$ for some $2<q_0\le p$: for $n>2$ take $q_0=\min(p,2n/(n-2))$, and for $n=2$ take $q_0=p$. Set $h_0=f+\lambda u\in L^{q_0}$. Theorem 19.7 gives a strong solution $z_0\in W^{2,q_0}\cap W^{1,q_0}_0$ of $(\lambda-\Delta)z_0=h_0$. The original $u$ solves the same shifted equation weakly; because $z_0\in W^{1,q_0}_0$ is the $W^{1,q_0}$ limit of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ functions and $q_0>2$ on bounded $\Omega$, the same approximants converge in $W^{1,2}$, so $z_0\in H^1_0$. Testing the difference against itself gives $\int_\Omega(|D(z_0-u)|^2+\lambda|z_0-u|^2)=0$. Thus $u=z_0$ and $u\in W^{2,q_0}$. If $q_0<p$, Sobolev embedding raises $u$ to $L^{q_1}$, where $q_1=\min(p,nq_0/(n-2q_0))$ when $2q_0<n$; if $2q_0=n$, use the embedding into every finite $L^r$ and take $q_1=p$, and if $2q_0>n$ use the $L^\infty$ embedding and take $q_1=p$. Repeat the shifted-equation argument at each exponent. The subcritical reciprocals decrease by $2/n$, so after finitely many steps the exponent reaches $p$; cap every step at $p$ so that $f\in L^p$ remains in the required $L^{q_i}$. This proves $u\in W^{2,p}\cap W^{1,p}_0$. Now the a priori estimate [[thm-global-w-two-p-dirichlet-estimate]] applies and gives the displayed bound. Finally, weak integration by parts identifies the regular distributions of -Δu and f; Countable-Choice injectivity gives -Δu=f almost everywhere ([[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). The bridge from Haller-Dintelmann's strong solvability theorem to the given weak solution is the shifted equation and energy uniqueness, not an assumption of $W^{2,p}$ regularity.

items.title: The Schauder estimate on a quadratic Poisson solution: radius powers balance
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice when invoking the estimate supplier for $n\ge2$. Let $n\ge1$, $0<\alpha<1$, $c\ne0$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ and $u(x):=\dfrac{c\,(R^2-|x-x_0|^2)}{2n}$. Then $-\Delta u\equiv c$ on $B_R(x_0)$ and $u=0$ on $\partial B_R(x_0)$. On the inner ball $B_{R/2}(x_0)$ one computes exactly
$$\sup_{B_{R/2}}|u|=\frac{|c|R^2}{2n},\qquad \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{B_{R/2}}|D^\beta u|=\frac{|c|R}{2n},\qquad |D^2u|\equiv\frac{|c|}{n},\qquad [D^2u]_{0,\alpha;B_{R/2}}=0,$$
so that
$$\|u\|^*_{2,\alpha;B_{R/2}(x_0)}=\frac{|c|R^2}{n},\qquad \|u\|_{\infty;B_R}+R^2\|Lu\|_{\infty;B_R}+R^{2+\alpha}[Lu]_{0,\alpha;B_R}=|c|R^2\Bigl(\frac1{2n}+1\Bigr),$$
for the operator $L=\Delta$ (so that $Lu=\Delta u=-c$). Both sides are proportional to $|c|R^2$ with constants independent of $R$: the radius powers balance exactly. The example also verifies the dilation identity $\|u\|^*_{2,\alpha;B_{R/2}(x_0)}=\|u(x_0+R\,\cdot)\|^*_{2,\alpha;B_{1/2}(0)}$ of [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]].
items.strategy: Differentiate the quadratic twice: $\partial_iu=-c(x_i-x_{0,i})/n$, $\partial_i\partial_ju=-c\delta_{ij}/n$, hence $\Delta u=-c$ and $-\Delta u=c$. Evaluate the scaled norm at the centre and on the half-ball, use $[D^2u]_{0,\alpha}=0$ because $D^2u$ is constant, and compare with the right-hand side of the Schauder estimate; repeat after the change of variables $z=(x-x_0)/R$ to display the dilation identity. The computation is the scaling check recorded in [S] Exercise 8.18 and [V] (3.11).

items.title: A non-Dini continuous Poisson source can destroy the continuity of the second derivatives
items.statement: The assertion that continuity of a compactly supported source $f$ suffices for the Newtonian potential $Nf$ to be of class $C^2$ with continuous second derivatives is false; the counterexample and its verification are in the next section.
items.strategy: Choose $\eta\in C^\infty([0,\infty);[0,1])$ equal to $1$ through radius $1/4$ and smoothly zero by radius $1/3$, and set $h(r)=\eta(r)/\log(1/r)$ for $r>0$ in the support. This makes the radial profile continuous at $0$ and smooth for positive radii, so the source is smooth away from the origin and the localized piece $\chi f$ in the off-origin argument is genuinely in $C_c^\infty$. First prove $Nf\in C^1$: split the difference quotient of the logarithmic kernel into $|z|\le2|h|$ and its complement; the near part is $O(|h||\log|h||)$ and Taylor's formula bounds the far remainder by $C|h||z|^{-2}$, whose integral is $O(|h|\log(1/|h|))$. The first derivative convolution is continuous by translating the variable and applying dominated convergence to the locally integrable kernels $\Phi$ and $\nabla\Phi$. The kernel identity $\partial_1\partial_1\Phi(z)=\cos(2\theta)/(2\pi|z|^2)$ with $z_1^2-z_2^2=|z|^2\cos2\theta$ gives the truncated polar integral $\frac1{2\pi}\int_\varepsilon^{1/4}h(r)r^{-1}dr\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^22\theta\,d\theta+O(1)=\frac12\int_\varepsilon^{1/4}h(r)r^{-1}dr+O(1)$, which diverges like $\frac12\log\log(1/\varepsilon)$. For $x\ne0$, split $f=\chi f+(1-\chi)f$ with $\chi=1$ on a smaller ball and supported on a larger ball avoiding the origin; the first potential is classical for smooth compact data, while the second has a smooth kernel separated from the support and is smooth by differentiation under the integral sign. The difference quotient of $\partial_1Nf$ at $0$ has the same diverging principal term and an $O(1)$ remainder, proving failure of a finite second derivative.

items.title: The Schauder estimate fails at the H\"older endpoint $\alpha=1$
items.statement: The interior Schauder estimate of [[thm-interior-schauder-estimate-for-uniformly-elliptic-equations]] does not extend to the endpoint $\alpha=1$: there is no constant $C<\infty$ such that $[D^2Nf]_{C^{0,1}(\mathbb R^2)}\le C\|f\|_{C^{0,1}(\mathbb R^2)}$ for every compactly supported Lipschitz source $f$ and its Newtonian potential $Nf$. The explicit counterexample below uses a Lipschitz source whose angular profile is the degree-one homogeneous mode $r\cos3\theta$; the second derivatives inherit an $r\log r$ term, which tends to zero but is not Lipschitz at the origin. Wang's theory gives the sharp bound with the logarithm $|x||\log|x||$ and the example shows that this logarithm cannot be removed.
items.strategy: Use the explicit source in the statement; its angular factor is the degree-one homogeneous mode $r\cos(3\theta)$. Directly, $\Delta(r^3\log r\cos(3\theta))=6r\cos(3\theta)$, so $p=-\frac16r^3\log r\cos(3\theta)$ is a local solution of $-\Delta p=f$. The small-circle flux vanishes at the origin. The difference $Nf-p$ is harmonic and hence smooth by [[thm-harmonic-functions-are-real-analytic]], so its Hessian is locally Lipschitz and cannot cancel the $-x_1\log x_1$ term in $\partial_{11}p(x_1,0)$. This proves endpoint failure directly; [W] Theorem 1 still supplies the upper log-Lipschitz modulus, but no inaccessible Burch example or unproved dyadic construction is needed for this counterexample.

items.title: The Riesz-transform formula for second derivatives of the Laplacian
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$ and $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$. Then, as tempered distributions (equivalently, as $L^2$ classes almost everywhere),
$$\partial_i\partial_ju=-R_iR_j(\Delta u)=R_iR_j(-\Delta u)\qquad(i,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}),$$
where $R_1,\dots,R_n$ are the Riesz transforms of [[def-riesz-transforms-on-euclidean-space]]; the symbol of $R_iR_j$ is $-\xi_i\xi_j/|\xi|^2$ off the origin, and combining the $L^p$ bounds of [[cor-riesz-transforms-are-bounded-on-lp]] gives
$$\|\partial_i\partial_ju\|_{L^p}\le C_{n,p}^2\,\|\Delta u\|_{L^p}\qquad(1<p<\infty).$$
For $n=1$ the identity reads $u''=-R_1R_1u''$ and is consistent because $R_1^2=-\mathrm{id}$ makes both sides equal $u''$.
items.strategy: On the Fourier side $\widehat{\partial_i\partial_ju}=(i\xi_i)(i\xi_j)\hat u=-\xi_i\xi_j\hat u$, while $R_iR_j$ has multiplier $(-i\xi_i/|\xi|)(-i\xi_j/|\xi|)=-\xi_i\xi_j/|\xi|^2$ and $\widehat{\Delta u}=-|\xi|^2\hat u$ off the origin, so $\widehat{R_iR_j(-\Delta u)}=-\xi_i\xi_j\hat u=\widehat{\partial_i\partial_ju}$; equality holds in $\mathcal S'$ by [[thm-fourier-differentiation-and-multiplication-identities-on-tempered-distributions]]. The $L^p$ bound is the composition of the two published Riesz bounds (each at most $C_{n,p}$); this is the Riesz-transform route to the $W^{2,p}$ estimate sketched in [S] §7.6 and used in [V] Theorem 3.7, and it independently verifies the whole-space Hessian estimate proved on this page.

items.title: Boundary $W^{2,p}$ regularity needs more than Lipschitz boundary
items.statement:
A weak-solution regularity assertion that replaces the $C^{1,1}$ boundary hypothesis by mere Lipschitz regularity is false; this does not refute the a priori estimate [[thm-global-w-two-p-dirichlet-estimate]], whose hypothesis already requires $u\in W^{2,p}$. The reentrant sector below is a bounded Lipschitz domain, but not a $C^{1,1}$ domain at its vertex. Let $\Omega_\omega=\{(r,\theta):0<r<1,\ 0<\theta<\omega\}$ with $\omega\in(\pi,2\pi)$, put $\gamma=\pi/\omega\in(1/2,1)$, and define $U=r^\gamma\sin(\gamma\theta)$. Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\zeta$ supported in $B_{1/2}$ and equal to $1$ near $0$, and let $v=\zeta U$. Choose $r_0>0$ so that $\zeta=1$ for $r<r_0$. Then $v\in H^1_0(\Omega_\omega)$, $f:=-\Delta v\in C^\infty(\Omega_\omega)\cap L^\infty(\Omega_\omega)\subset L^p(\Omega_\omega)$ for every finite $p$, and $-\Delta v=f$ weakly. However, $|D^2v|\asymp r^{\gamma-2}$ near $0$, so
$$\int_0^{r_0}r^{p(\gamma-2)+1}\,dr=\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\ge\frac{2}{2-\gamma}=\frac{2\omega}{2\omega-\pi}.$$
Hence this weak solution is not in $W^{2,p}$ for those exponents (in particular not in $H^2$). The reentrant corner shows why weak boundary regularity requires more than a Lipschitz chart.
items.strategy: In polar coordinates $U$ is harmonic and vanishes on both straight sides. Since $\gamma>1/2$, $U$ and its gradient are square-integrable near the vertex. To verify $v\in H^1_0$, first cut it off for $r<2\varepsilon$; the squared $H^1$ error is $O(\varepsilon^{2\gamma})$. Then use angular cutoffs vanishing within distance $\delta$ of each side; since $U=O(r^\gamma\theta)$ near a side, their squared gradient error is $O(\delta)$. The outer radial cutoff already vanishes near $r=1$. These approximants are supported compactly inside the sector and can be mollified there, proving $v\in H^1_0$. The forcing $-\Delta(\zeta U)$ is supported where $\nabla\zeta\ne0$, an annulus separated from the vertex, so it is smooth and bounded on the open sector but its support is not compactly contained in $\Omega_\omega$. The distributional equation holds on compactly supported tests because $v$ is smooth in the open sector; density extends it to $H^1_0$. On the smaller sector where $\zeta=1$, $|D^2v|\asymp r^{\gamma-2}$, and polar integration gives the exact divergence threshold displayed. This refutes weak-solution regularity on Lipschitz domains, not the a priori estimate for functions already in $W^{2,p}$; compare [T] Example 10.1 and [V] Theorem 3.8.

items.title: The method of continuity on a constant-coefficient one-dimensional path
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and fix $0<\alpha<1$. Let $\Omega=(0,\pi)$, $X:=\{u\in C^{2,\alpha}([0,\pi]):u(0)=u(\pi)=0\}$, $Y:=C^{0,\alpha}([0,\pi])$ and, for $c>0$ and $t\in[0,1]$, $L_tu:=-u''-tc\,u$. Then every $L_t$ is a bounded operator $X\to Y$, $L_0=-d^2/dx^2$ is bijective, and the bijectivity set is $I=\{t\in[0,1]:tc\notin\{k^2:k\ge1\}\}$: for $tc<1$ the eigenfunction expansion
$$u(x)=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{f_k}{k^2-tc}\sin(kx),\qquad f_k=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(kx)\,dx,$$
converges absolutely and uniformly together with its first derivative, defines an element of $X$ with $L_tu=f$ and obeys the uniform bound $\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}\le C(1-tc)^{-1}\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$, while at $tc=k_0^2$ the kernel is spanned by $\sin(k_0x)$ and the range is the proper closed subspace $\{f:\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(k_0x)\,dx=0\}$. In this model one computes directly that $I$ is open in $[0,1]$, that $I$ is relatively closed on every subinterval on which all the operators are injective, and that the uniform estimate fails on every interval that meets the spectrum.
items.strategy: Use the Dirichlet sine eigenbasis and integrate by parts to identify the kernel and range at each resonance. For each non-resonant parameter (and for resonant data orthogonal to the resonant mode), divide the Fourier coefficients by $k^2-tc$ away from resonance. The Hölder coefficient decay makes only the solution and first-derivative series absolutely and uniformly convergent; a low/high-frequency split gives $u\in C^{0,\alpha}$. Identify $u″=-f-tcu$ distributionally from the $L^2$ convergence of the sine partial sums, then use the continuous right-hand side and the zero-derivative distribution theorem to obtain $u\in C^{2,\alpha}$. In $tc<1$, the denominator bound yields the stated $C^{2,\alpha}$ inverse estimate; the finite spectral set gives openness and relative closedness directly.

items.title: Bounded measurable coefficients do not give Schauder estimates
items.statement: The assertion that uniform ellipticity with merely bounded (even bounded continuous) principal coefficients suffices for a $C^{2,\alpha}$ conclusion for classical $C^2$ solutions of $Lu=f$ is false; the counterexample below exhibits a bounded continuous uniformly elliptic $L$, a classical $C^2$ solution of $Lu=1$, and a coefficient that fails to make $D^2u$ $\alpha$-Hölder for any exponent larger than the coefficient modulus. This does not contradict the interior Schauder theorem of this page, which assumes $C^{0,\alpha}$ principal coefficients.
items.strategy: Differentiate the displayed one-variable integral twice to obtain $u''(t)=(1+|t|^\beta)^{-1}$, then substitute into the nondivergence operator to get $Lu=1$. Uniform ellipticity follows from $1\le1+|x_1|^\beta\le2$ on $B_1$. The quotient $|u''(h)-u''(0)|/|h|^\alpha=|h|^{\beta-\alpha}/(1+|h|^\beta)$ diverges as $h\to0$, so $D^2u$ is not $C^{0,\alpha}$. The example weakens exactly the principal coefficient regularity and uses no divergence-form interpretation.

items.title: Freezing cannot absorb a fixed oscillation on arbitrarily small balls
items.statement: Freezing coefficients is a stable device only when the coefficient oscillation at small scales actually vanishes. The assertion that the Hölder (or continuity) hypothesis on the principal coefficients in the freezing and Schauder arguments can be replaced by mere boundedness, or that the freezing radius alone can make an arbitrary fixed oscillation absorbable, is false: for a jump coefficient the freezing error is not even $\alpha$-Hölder at any scale, so no choice of the freezing radius makes the error term absorbable by the scaled norm.
items.strategy: For $x_0$ with $x_{0,1}=0$ the ball $B_\rho(x_0)$ meets both half-spaces $\{x_1>0\}$ and $\{x_1<0\}$ for every $\rho>0$, so $a$ takes both values $a_0\pm b$ on the ball and the oscillation is $2b$. Pairs of points at distance $\delta>0$ straddling the interface have $|a(x)-a(y)|=2b$, so the sup defining $[a]_{0,\alpha;B_\rho(x_0)}$ is over ratios $2b\,t^{-\alpha}$ with $t\to0$, giving $+\infty$. Compare the freezing absorption requirement $\rho^\alpha K\le\varepsilon$ in [S] (8.14)-(8.15) and the modulus $\epsilon(\delta)$ in [V] Part I, neither of which can be met.
